title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock

understand.restatement: Choose one day to buy and a later day to sell. Return the largest possible profit, or 0 if every trade would lose money or no trade is possible.
understand.inputs: A list prices, where prices[i] is the stock price on day i.
understand.outputs: A nonnegative number representing the maximum profit.
constraints: Make at most one purchase and one sale.
The sale must happen after the purchase.
Return 0 when no profitable trade exists.
Assume nonnegative integer prices; empty and single-element lists return 0.
clarifying_questions: Can the list be empty or contain only one price?
What are the maximum list length and price value?

examples.explanation: Buy on day 1 at price 1 and sell on day 4 at price 6, using zero-based day indices.
Prices only fall, so making no trade is best.
There is no later day on which to sell.

pattern.name: Greedy
pattern.why: For each selling day, the best buying day is the cheapest earlier day. In the story, the price lanterns are daily prices, and Mira's two notebook entries are the cheapest price seen and the best profit found.
pattern.recognize: When choosing an ordered pair to maximize a difference, ask whether one running minimum can summarize all earlier choices.

approach.brute_force: Try every buying day and every later selling day. Keep the largest positive difference. This takes O(n²) time and O(1) extra space.
approach.optimized: Use two scalar variables, not an additional data structure: lowest stores the cheapest price seen, and best stores the largest profit found. Scan left to right. First consider selling at today's price using lowest, then update lowest. All earlier buying prices are at least lowest, so none can give a better profit for today's sale. The first iteration contributes only 0, not a real same-day trade.
approach.optimized_pseudocode:
if prices is empty:
    return 0
lowest = prices[0]
best = 0
for price in prices:
    best = max(best, price - lowest)
    lowest = min(lowest, price)
return best

complexity.explanation: Each of the n prices is visited once, with constant work per visit. Only two running values are stored, regardless of input size.
follow_ups: How would you return the buying and selling day indices as well?
What changes if you may complete unlimited non-overlapping trades?
How would you handle a transaction fee or a cooldown after selling?

scenes.caption: Mira enters the harbor market, where six lanterns reveal prices on six successive days: 7, 1, 5, 3, 6, and 4. She carries one trading permit and a little notebook. The lanterns glow in order; tomorrow's stall cannot be visited today.

“One purchase, one later sale,” the harbormaster reminds her. Mira wants the biggest gain, but she may keep her coins if nothing pays. She eyes the lantern marked 1 and the later lantern marked 6, wondering whether their five-coin gap is unbeatable.

Before committing, Mira sketches every possible earlier purchase and later sale. Lines crowd her notebook as she compares 7 with every later lantern, then repeats for 1 and the others. “This takes forever,” she sighs. Even worse, selling at 7 after buying at 1 would reverse time.

question.prompt: Why can't Mira buy at 1 and sell at 7?
options: The sale would come before the purchase.
She must buy at the highest price.
question.hint: Read the lanterns from left to right as passing days.

scenes.caption: Then Mira notices a shortcut: “For any sale, only the cheapest earlier offer matters!” Walking forward, she replaces 7 with 1 in her notebook. The lantern at 5 offers profit 4; the one at 3 offers only 2. Her best gain stays 4.

question.prompt: After reaching price 3, what should Mira remember?
question.hint: A less profitable selling day does not erase a better earlier opportunity.

scenes.caption: At 6, Mira records profit 5; at 4, nothing improves. She closes her notebook, triumphant: buy at 1, sell at 6. Her coding solution needs no additional structure, just scalars storing the lowest price and best profit; constant-time comparisons and updates make one forward scan enough.

code_hotspots.why: The loop visits every price exactly once.
A subtraction and maximum update take constant time per price.
The running minimum is updated in constant time.

frames.note: Initialize with 7; the first iteration yields 0 and represents no trade.
Selling at 1 is unprofitable, but 1 becomes the cheapest purchase for future days.
Selling at 5 after buying at 1 improves the best profit to 4.
Profit 2 does not beat the best profit of 4.
Selling at 6 improves the best profit to 5.
The final price offers only profit 3, so return 5.
